newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION-INDIA ECONOMIC REFORMS - BY MERRILL LYNCH.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-INDIA ECONOMIC REFORMS - BY MERRILL LYNCH.

text.p: The following is an extract from India Economic Reforms - Consolidation and Acceleration, a report by Merrill Lynch economists John Praveen and Donald Straszheim.
OUTLOOK AND CHALLENGES
GROWTH: SOLID, TRENDING UP

Growth has been solid in the last few years and in 1995/96, GDP growth at 7 percent was higher than forecast. Among its objectives, the United Front government has target an annual growth rate of 7 percent over the next decade, led by a 12 percent growth rate in the industrial sector.

Further, the strong overall growth performance in 1995/96 was despite sluggish growth in the agriculture sector. If the agriculture sector revives in response to the incentives in the budget, while the industry and services sector continue their performance, GDP growth could easily come in around 6.5 percent in 1996/97.
Prospects for India's exports are good since recoveries are forecast for Japan and Europe which account for 34 percent of India's exports.

Faster export growth should contribute to GDP growth. Another positive for growth is the expected strong capital inflows which should facilitate a higher rate of investment than permitted by domestic savings.
INFLATION: TRENDING DOWN
We expect inflation to continue to trend down and remain in the 6-7 percent range. On the positive side, the following factors are expected to dampen inflation:
** The RBI currently has greater flexibility in monetary management and can be expected to tighten monetary policy to control inflation.

In fact, the Finance Minister himself has been publicly encouraging the RBI to hold the line on inflation: "It is the duty of the RBI to keep inflation in check by ensuring that money supply growth does not exceed the target set for the current year."
** Helping the RBI dampen inflationary pressure by controlling money supply growth is the general fiscal consolidation and reduction in monetization of the fiscal deficit.

** As structural reform leads to more competition in electricity supply, telephone services and public transport, it could have a significant downward pressure on the prices of these non-tradeable goods, and
** In the case of tradeable goods, as reforms make the economy more open, international competition can be expected to exert downward pressure on prices.
However, the following factors could put upward pressure on prices:
** Strong growth leading to demand-pull pressures;
** Increases in wage and salaries in urban areas could compound this demand-pull inflation by adding more cost-push pressures, and

** Increases in various administered prices: Officials have made it clear that the present public distribution system for food needs to be revamped and food subsidies have to be targeted to rural areas.

Upward adjustments in food prices are likely to fall on the urban consumer which should be reflected in the consumer price index for industrial workers. Further, administered prices of other items of mass consumption - fuel, electricity, public transport, education and medical services - may also be adjusted up as part of fiscal consolidation.
Increases in administered prices, to more accurately reflect the market value of these goods and services, may be the principal source of inflation in the medium-term.
INTEREST RATES: DOWNWARD PRESSURE

While interest rates have tended to be high due to strong private sector credit demand and continued large government borrowing requirement, the following reasons give us optimism that interest rates will come down:
** Further fiscal consolidation leading to lower government borrowing from the market;

** To the extent financial markets feel the government is taking credible steps to reduce the fiscal deficits, there could be a reduction in the risk premium on government borrowing, putting downward pressure on interest rates;
** The steady decline in inflation should lead to downward adjustment of inflationary expectations, in turn, leading to lower interest rates;
** Lower SLR and CRR should enable banks to have more funds available to meet credit demand, easing pressures on interest rates, and
** Increased competition in the banking sector should exert downward pressure on interest margins.
CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT: AT SUSTAINABLE LEVELS

In the last two years, robust industrial growth has fueled strong import growth and a widening of the trade and current account deficits. The modest widening of the external deficits are not cause for concern for three reasons:
** The recent deficits are still significantly smaller than the current account deficits during the late 1980s which were over 2.5 percent of GDP;
** There has been a significant improvement in coverage of import payments through export earnings, and
** There is a reduced dependence on debt-creating capital inflows to finance the current account deficit.
CURRENCY: STABLE

We expect the Indian rupee to be stable around Rs/US$ 35-36. With a modest current account deficit fully financed by strong capital inflows, the rupee is not expected to be under the kind of pressure experience in late 1995 and early 1996.
Given the inflation differential between India and its major trading partners, the rupee should depreciate around 4 percent during the next year.
INFRASTRUCTURE CHALLENGES
Infrastructure deficiencies and bottlenecks are likely to be a major constraint to India sustaining the pace of growth and stepping it up to the pace of the East Asian countries.

Over the last 40 years, India built up a vast infrastructure in electricity supply, transportation, ports and telecommunications. Installed electricity generating capacity has risen from 2,300 MW in 1950 to 79,000 MW in 1993. Railway freight grew from 73 million tons in 1950 to 350 million tons in 1993.
Cargo handled at major ports increased from 19.2 million tons in 1950 to 167 million tons in 1993. As of 1993, 17,790 telephone exchanges had a combined capacity of 8.4 million telephone lines.
However, the infrastructure provision falls far short of the demand for these infrastructure services. By international standards, India's infrastructure stock is low.

In 1993, India had an infrastructure stock of little over $500 per capita, lower than most Asian competitors. In addition to a low stock, poor maintenance and lack of repairs have resulted in sub optimal performance from the existing stock. Dilapidated and congested roads, frequent power outages and faulty telephone connections are a daily occurrence.

Part of the infrastructure problem has been that because of the public sector monopoly in the infrastructure sector, the strained fiscal position in recent years has meant less investment in infrastructure development.
Economic liberalisation ended the public sector monopoly in the provision of infrastructure services and opened up many of these industries in the infrastructure sector to private investment.
Electricity generation, for example, was opened up to private investment in the mid-1980s with the government guaranteeing a minimum rate on investment.

During the 1990s, several measures have been taken to facilitate the entry of the private sector and foreign investment into power, telecommunications, aviation, ports and roads. However, a combination of administrative delays and intra-governmental tussles, several infrastructure projects, including some 40 approved new power projects with a total capacity of almost 28,000 MW, are believed be held up for implementation.
Further, private sector and foreign interest in infrastructure has been lukewarm at best.
Thus serious infrastructure deficiencies remain and addressing them is likely to be a major challenge for the government in the near- to medium-term.

The new UF government has accorded a high priority to easing the infrastructure constraints. In the CMP, the UF government has declared that investment in infrastructure will be stepped up from the current level of 3.5-4 percent of GDP to at least 6 percent of GDP over the next few years.

The cumulative investment requirement in infrastructure over the next 5 years are estimated to be at least $200 billion. The domestic private sector and foreign capital are expected to play a big role in mobilizing these resources for infrastructure investment. The challenge of India's infrastructure needs is a major opportunity for foreign investment.
FISCAL POLICY CHALLENGES

The new United Front Government is committed to fiscal prudence and its objective is to reduce the central government fiscal deficit to under 4 percent of GDP in the medium-term (about 2 years). The government will have to overcome the following expenditure and revenue challenges in meeting the fiscal targets.
** Expenditure constraints

In 1995/96, interest payment on government debt (38 percent), grants to states and union territories (16 percent), defense expenditure (13.3 percent) and subsidies (9 percent) combined, absorbed about 76.6 percent of federal government expenditure. Reducing any of these expenditures are difficult:
* Interest payments are contractual obligation on past debt and have to be honored;
* Grants to states and union territories are constitutionally mandated thus, must be met;
* Defense expenditure has already been reduced and further cuts cannot be undertaken without compromising national security, and
* Subsidies are politically sensitive and their reduction requires political muscle and resolve.
** Composition of Federal Government's Current Expenditure
This leaves only 23.4 percent of expenditure from which

to achieve any significant savings. Given this constraint and the clear realization that public expenditure needs to be trimmed further to achieve deficit reduction, Finance Minister Chidambaram, in the 1996/97 budget, announced the appointment of a commission to examine expenditure cuts. Further, the government plans to issue a white paper (i.e., policy paper) on subsidies so the issue can be debated and a consensus built on both the level and targeting of subsidies. If the proposed expenditure committee and the white paper on subsidies generate a public consensus on expenditure cuts and the level of subsidies, the government may acquire the political muscle to push through expenditure cuts and help deficit reduction.
** Revenue Challenges

Among capital receipts, the 1996/97 budget includes a public sector divestment target of 50 billion rupees. This target appears ambitious in light of last year's experience. In 1995/96, public sector divestment realized only 13.9 billion rupees against a budget estimate of 70 billion rupees. Further, other than the MAT, there are no significant measures to raise revenues, while expenditure cuts have been postponed. This carries the risk that the deficit could overshoot if the public sector divestment target is not met.
** Buoyant Direct Taxes & a Setback to Indirect Taxes

Further, revenues have been sticky. The tax reforms have improved collection of direct taxes, with central government revenues from direct taxes rising to 3.1 percent of GDP in 1995/96 from 2.1 percent in 1990/91 and 2.1 percent average during 1985/90. Direct tax revenues to both the centre and the states increased to 3.7 percent of GDP in 1995/96 from 2.7 percent in 1990/91.
** India: Sources of Tax Revenue

Indirect taxes have been less buoyant, declining from 8.1 percent in 1990/91 to 7.2 percent in 1995/96 at the centre and from 13.8 percent of GDP to 12.4 percent for the centre and states combined. The setback to indirect taxes, which make up 75 percent of total revenues of the central government and 80 percent of general government revenue, are responsible for a decline in total tax revenue receipts to 10.2 percent of GDP in 1995/96 from an average of 11.1 percent during 1985/90.
** General Government Current Revenue

Despite the setbacks to revenue receipts, there is significant scope for higher revenue receipts for the government. India's general government revenue, was under 20 percent of GDP in 1995/96. This is less than half the level in the European and the smaller OECD countries and about half the level in the G-7 nations. The share of government revenue in India is also one of the lowest among the emerging markets. Better implementations of tax reforms and more efficient tax collection should enable the government to have a higher revenue intake which, in turn, should help reduce the fiscal and revenue deficits.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author only. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters)
